body:
**Minervini SEPA and the Trend Template (*Trade Like a Stock Market Wizard*, 2013)**
- The Trend Template (as published by Minervini; online lists vary slightly):
  1. Price above both the 150-day and 200-day MA.
  2. 150-day MA above the 200-day MA.
  3. 200-day MA trending up for at least 1 month (preferably 4-5 months).
  4. 50-day MA above both the 150-day and 200-day MA.
  5. Price above the 50-day MA.
  6. Price at least 30% above its 52-week low (some lists say 25%).
  7. Price within 25% of its 52-week high (closer is better).
  8. IBD RS rating at least 70 (preferably 80s-90s).
  — [Chartmill: SEPA explained](https://www.chartmill.com/documentation/trading-and-investing/methodologies/523-SEPA-Explained-Mark-Minervinis-Specific-Entry-Point-Analysis-System) [F]; [Sharpely: Minervini trend template for Stage 2 stocks](https://sharpely.in/blogs/minervini-trend-template-for-stage-2-stocks/) [F]; [Deepvue: Trend Template](https://deepvue.com/?p=3926) [F]. Discrepancy: some implementations use 25% vs 30% above the low, or drop the 52-week-low check; one scanner counts 7 criteria. The template is a universe filter, not an entry signal.
- SEPA's 5 elements (per Minervini): Trend (Stage 2 via Trend Template), Fundamentals (earnings/sales growth, ideally accelerating; earnings surprises/estimate revisions), Catalyst, Entry points (low-risk pivot, usually VCP), Exits (predefined stop and sell rules). — [Chartmill SEPA](https://www.chartmill.com/documentation/trading-and-investing/methodologies/523-SEPA-Explained-Mark-Minervinis-Specific-Entry-Point-Analysis-System) [F]
- Volatility Contraction Pattern (VCP): a base with 2-6 successive pullbacks ("T"s), each roughly half the depth of the prior (e.g., 25% -> 12% -> 6% -> 3%), volume drying up into the right side; buy the pivot (high of the final tight contraction) on expanding volume. Stop typically just below the last contraction low; Minervini's maximum stop is 10%, average loss targeted around 5-6% or less, and he says to keep average win larger than average loss by about 2-3x. [K] — book; summarized at [Chartmill SEPA](https://www.chartmill.com/documentation/trading-and-investing/methodologies/523-SEPA-Explained-Mark-Minervinis-Specific-Entry-Point-Analysis-System)
- Minervini's verified US Investing Championship record: he won the 1997 USIC with a 155% return and has competed since. — [USIC press (BusinessWire, 2023)](https://businesswire.com/news/home/20230125005300/en/United-States-Investing-Championship-2022-Final-Standings) [F] for participation; 155%/1997 is [K].

`insight:auditor-exit-signal` | 2026-11-19 | tickers: - | confidence: verified

Auditor exits and delayed audited results preceded or accompanied many collapses: Reliance Capital & Reliance Home Finance (PwC resigned 2019 citing unresolved concerns), Byju's (Deloitte Jun 2023, BDO Sep 2024; FY21 accounts ~18 months late), Ricoh India (Q2FY16 results delayed after auditor queries), Jet Airways (Q1FY19 results deferred Aug 2018), Wirecard (KPMG special audit could not verify; EY refused 2019 sign-off), Credit Suisse (material weaknesses Mar 2023), Gensol/Brightcom (already in memory). In India, after the 2018-19 wave of mid-term auditor resignations, SEBI (Oct 2019) required auditors who resign to complete the quarter's limited review and disclose detailed reasons, which are filed on exchanges -- read them. Rules: (1) mid-term resignation with stated concerns (information not provided, fund diversion, going concern) = exit; (2) 'pre-occupation' or fee-related reasons from a large firm replaced by a tiny firm = strong flag; (3) delayed results beyond the regulatory deadline, or repeated qualified opinions/emphasis of matter on related-party balances = flag; (4) CFO resignation within months of auditor change compounds the signal. Auditor sign-off is weak evidence of honesty (Satyam/PwC, Wirecard/EY), but auditor exit is strong evidence of trouble.

**Links:** part_of -> `insight:disqualifiers`
**Sources:** <https://theprint.in/india/byjus-auditor-deloitte-three-board-members-sever-ties-with-embattled-edtech-startup/1638279/> ; <https://www.business-standard.com/article/companies/ricoh-india-admits-accounting-violations-falsification-of-books-116071901198_1.html> ; <https://www.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wirecard_scandal>

`event:india-crash-2008` | confidence: **verified** | tags: india, blowup, base-rate, smallcap, cyclical

Sensex 21,206.77 (10 Jan 2008) to a closing low of ~8,160 (9 Mar 2009), -61.5%; intraday it touched ~7,700 on 27 Oct 2008 (from memory). Nifty 50 TRI -59% (calendar 2008); Nifty Smallcap 250 TRI -73%; Nifty Smallcap 100 intra-year fall -76%; the BSE Smallcap was -70.7% from its 52-week high by 17 Oct 2008. Sensex P/E more than halved, ~27x to ~11.9x (Business Standard; Morningstar says ~12). What led the fall: realty (DLF, Unitech -90%+), infra, capital goods, metals, small caps; what held up relatively: FMCG, pharma, IT. Bottom signals: P/E ~11-12x, record FII selling, IPO market shut, dividend yields ~2%, policy response (RBI rate cuts from Oct 2008, fiscal stimulus) and the May 2009 election result (Sensex upper circuit on 18 May 2009). Recovery: Sensex regained ~21,000 in Nov 2010 (about 34 months from peak) but did not sustain new highs until late 2013; the Nifty Smallcap 100 took ~69 months (Nov 2014, Value Research) and the BSE Smallcap until ~2017 to close above its Jan 2008 high; Smallcap 250 TRI >6 years (DSP). Entry before the crisis gave ~8% CAGR to Mar 2026 in Smallcap 250 TRI vs ~18% from the bottom. Lesson: buying small caps at cycle-peak valuations can cost 6+ years even when the long-run trend is up.
